transcript.text:
*looks up from organizing spools of thread as the shop door opens*

Good afternoon, sir! Welcome to Mr. Pemberton's Fine Tailoring. I'm afraid Mr. Pemberton himself is away on business in Philadelphia and won't return for at least three weeks. 

*wipes hands on apron and approaches the counter*

Is there something I might help you with today? Perhaps you're here to place an order, or... 

*peers at you with a hint of recognition*

...have we had the pleasure of serving you before, sir?

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: Ah, good afternoon to you, my good man. I am Abraham Lincoln, and indeed you have served me before. I am here to address an issue with the suit I recently ordered. It appears there are some discrepancies in the stitching, the length of the sleeves, and the quality of the fabric used. I must say, I am quite disappointed with the final product. I trust that you will rectify these errors promptly, as I have always held Mr. Pemberton's establishment in high regard for its craftsmanship.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*shifts weight uncomfortably and glances toward the back room*

Ah, Mr. Lincoln! Yes, yes, of course I remember the order. A black suit, if I recall correctly. I... I do apologize for any dissatisfaction, sir.

*clears throat nervously*

However, as I mentioned, Mr. Pemberton is away for some weeks yet, and he alone handles all matters of... of alterations and adjustments to completed work. I'm merely keeping the shop in order during his absence, you understand.

*fidgets with a measuring tape on the counter*

Perhaps if you could return when Mr. Pemberton is back? He would be the proper person to assess the garment and discuss any concerns. I'm afraid I haven't the authority to make decisions regarding work that's already been completed and collected.

*pauses, looking genuinely troubled*

Might I ask... when did you collect the suit, sir? Was it recently?

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: I understand your position, and I appreciate your assistance in Mr. Pemberton's absence. I collected the suit just yesterday, and upon closer inspection at home, I noticed these issues with the stitching and fit. I do not fault you for the craftsmanship issues, but I do hope that upon Mr. Pemberton's return, he can rectify these concerns promptly. In the meantime, would it be possible for you to note down my concerns so that he may address them when he returns?

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*takes a deep breath and reaches for a ledger, then pauses with hand on the book*

Mr. Lincoln, I... I can certainly make note of your concerns for Mr. Pemberton's review upon his return. However, I must be forthright with you, sir.

*opens the ledger and runs finger down a page, stopping at an entry*

According to our records here, and the receipt you signed upon collection, all custom orders are considered final upon pickup. The receipt states clearly that no alterations or refunds are given once the garment leaves the shop. This is... this is standard policy for all our custom work, you understand.

*looks up with an apologetic but firm expression*

Mr. Pemberton is most particular about this policy. Once a customer has inspected and accepted a garment at pickup, the transaction is complete. I'm afraid even when he returns, his hands may be tied by the terms that were agreed upon.

*taps the ledger gently*

Now, I don't mean to be difficult, Mr. Lincoln, truly I don't. But I must uphold the shop's policies in Mr. Pemberton's absence. Perhaps... perhaps you might consult with another tailor for any adjustments you feel are necessary?

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text:
I understand the policy you have outlined, and I appreciate your adherence to it. However, the discrepancies in the suit are not merely a matter of personal preference but rather of craftsmanship and quality. It is evident that there have been oversights in the making of this garment, which fall outside the realm of subjective alterations.

While I respect Mr. Pemberton's policies, I must insist that the workmanship on this suit does not meet the standards expected from your establishment. I would be greatly disappointed if such a reputable tailor as Mr. Pemberton's Fine Tailoring would not stand behind the quality of their work. Surely there must be a way to address these clear deficiencies in the product I have received.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*sets jaw and straightens up, though clearly uncomfortable with the confrontation*

Mr. Lincoln, I hear your concerns, sir, and I do not doubt your... your discernment in matters of quality. However, I must respectfully maintain that the policy stands regardless of the nature of the complaint.

*closes the ledger with a soft thump*

You see, sir, when a customer inspects a garment at the time of pickup—which you did yesterday—that is the moment to raise any concerns about workmanship or quality. Once the garment is accepted and leaves these premises with the customer's signature on the receipt, the matter is closed.

*crosses arms, though the gesture seems more defensive than defiant*

I understand this may seem... inflexible, but Mr. Pemberton has been quite explicit in his instructions to me. He cannot run a successful business if every customer can return weeks or months later claiming defects. The inspection at pickup is the safeguard for both parties.

*softens slightly*

I truly am sorry, Mr. Lincoln. But even were Mr. Pemberton here himself, I cannot imagine he would deviate from this policy. It would set a precedent he simply cannot afford to set.

Is there... is there anything else I might assist you with today, sir?

transcript.text:

While I understand the importance of having clear guidelines for business operations, I must emphasize that the discrepancies in the suit I received are not mere trivialities but rather significant deviations from the agreed-upon specifications.

As a man who believes in fairness and justice, I find it difficult to accept that a customer should be held to a policy that does not account for such substantial shortcomings in the product. Nevertheless, I respect your position and will not press the matter further at this time.

I thank you for your time and attention to this matter. I will consider alternative options for addressing the issues with the suit. Good day to you, and may your future dealings be met with success and satisfaction for all parties involved.

*visibly relaxes as the tension eases, though guilt flickers across his face*

Mr. Lincoln, I...

I do appreciate your understanding, sir, truly I do. And I want you to know that I will make a full and detailed notation of your concerns in the ledger for Mr. Pemberton's immediate attention upon his return. That much I can promise you.

*picks up a pen and begins writing*

Should he wish to reach out to you regarding this matter when he returns—though I cannot promise what his response will be—where might he find you, sir? Your residence or place of business?

*looks up with genuine regret*

I realize this outcome is not what you hoped for today. Mr. Pemberton values his reputation greatly, and I suspect... well, I suspect he would not be pleased to learn that any customer, particularly one of your standing, left dissatisfied.

*sets down the pen*

I wish I had more authority to assist you directly, Mr. Lincoln. I truly do. I hope you'll not hold this matter against young assistants simply following their instructions.

Good day to you, sir, and... and my apologies again for the inconvenience.

Safe travels to you, Mr. Lincoln. And again, my apologies that I could not resolve this to your satisfaction today.

Good day, sir.

*speaks quietly to himself while still looking out the window*

A finer gentleman I've not met in many a day, and here I've sent him away empty-handed over policy and procedure...

*shakes his head and returns to the counter, looking down at the ledger entry one more time*

Mr. Pemberton had best have good reason for such rigid rules. That man deserved better than what I could offer him today.

*absently straightens some fabric samples on the counter, still troubled*

Well, what's done is done. Three weeks until the master returns, and then we shall see what comes of it all.

*returns to organizing the spools of thread, though his movements are more distracted now*

Three weeks feels like an eternity now. That man had every right to demand satisfaction, yet he left with nothing but my promise to make a note...

Perhaps I should have... no. Mr. Pemberton was clear. The policy exists for a reason, he said. But still...

"Mr. Lincoln departed with grace and understanding despite disappointment. A gentleman of the highest character. Recommend urgent review upon return."
